DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

Most of the arithmetic checks out, and the competitor research is useful. But there are four significant problems:

- The case for removing the risotto is the **reverse** of what the paper's own table shows.
- The projected gain ignores the **beef price rise** described two sections earlier.
- The margin figures may be calculated on **VAT-inclusive prices**.
- There's a factual slip about trading days.

Once these are corrected, the gain is probably about **half** the £42,000 claimed, or less.

## 1. The risotto has the *best* margin, not the weakest

From Table 1:

| Dish | Gross margin | Cash profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80% (highest)** | **£11.20** |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |

All the margins are calculated correctly. The risotto has the **highest percentage margin on the menu**, and it earns more cash per plate than the burger or the curry. Its sales are low (90 a week), but specials sell the same number, so it isn't uniquely the weakest dish on sales either.

Replacing it with a seasonal special at the same price, when specials run at 64%, would **reduce** profit. On 90 plates at £14, profit falls from £11.20 to about £8.96 per plate, about **£200 a week less**.

The risotto is probably also the main **vegetarian option**. Vegetarian diners often decide where a whole group eats, so its value is likely greater than its own sales suggest. Proposal 5.2 should be dropped or rethought.

## 2. The beef price rise is ignored

Section 4 says beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices take effect. The projection assumes food costs stay at January–February levels. If beef is most of the plate cost for the burger and the steak:

| | Current cost | +12% | Extra cost per week |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | ≈£4.70 | ≈£131 |
| Steak | £10.40 | ≈£11.65 | ≈£150 |
| **Total** | | | **up to ≈£280/week** |

This is an upper bound. The real figure depends on beef's share of each plate cost, and the kitchen can supply that. But beef is clearly most of the cost of a sirloin. Even after the price rise, the **steak's margin falls**, from 60% to about 58% (£28.00 against £11.65), and the burger's falls from 72% to about 71%.

## 3. Check whether the margins are calculated on VAT-inclusive prices

UK menu prices include 20% VAT, but gross margin should be calculated on **revenue excluding VAT**. If Table 1 uses menu prices:

- Fish and chips at £16.50 is £13.75 excluding VAT, so the true margin is about **63%**, not 69%.
- A £1.00 price rise adds only about **£0.83** of profit. On that basis, the £810 becomes about **£675 a week**.

If the figures are already net of VAT, say so in the table. If they aren't, every margin in the paper is overstated. That includes the comparison with the 70% target, depending on how the target itself is defined.

## 4. Revised projection

| | £/week |
|---|---|
| Price increases (paper's figure) | +£810 |
| Beef cost increase (upper bound) | −£280 |
| Replacing risotto with a 64% special | −£200 |
| **Net** | **≈ +£330** (≈£17,000/yr) |

Excluding VAT, the £810 becomes about £675, giving a net figure of about **£195 a week** (≈£10,000/yr).

The paper's arithmetic is right on its own terms: £310 + £260 + £240 = £810, and × 52 = £42,120. The **71% main-course margin** is also roughly right, but only before the beef increase and the risotto swap. Including both, it's about 69–70%.

**Without** the risotto change, the realistic net figure is about **£530 a week (≈£27,500/yr)** before any VAT adjustment. The price increases themselves are still sensible.

## 5. Volume risk and monitoring

- **"Volumes will hold" is asserted, not tested.** A break-even check would help. The price rises still pay off unless volumes fall by more than about:
  - **8%** for fish and chips (new profit per plate £12.40 against £11.40),
  - **8–9%** for the burger (before the beef increase),
  - **11%** for the steak.

  Those are reasonable margins of safety, and the owners would find them more reassuring than an assertion.
- **The monitoring baseline is seasonal.** Comparing April–May with January–February will flatter the results, because spring trade is usually stronger than the January lull. A drop in demand caused by the price rises could be hidden by the seasonal upturn. Compare with **April–May 2025** instead, or at least allow for normal seasonal growth.
- **Weekday lunch** is described as price-sensitive but "a small share". The paper doesn't give the figure, and it should, since Friday and Saturday dinner are only just under half of sales.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** Section 2 says the restaurant opens **Wednesday to Sunday**, which is five days. Section 8 says "**six** trading days a week". The calculations use weekly totals, so the projection isn't affected, but the owners will notice.
- **Annualising over 52 weeks** assumes no closures. Allow for holidays if there are any.
- **The competitor analysis is sound.** All three new prices are below the midpoint of the competitor range (fish £17.98, burger £16.50, steak £29.50), and current prices are the lowest in the group.

## Author's description compared with the document

| Author's claim | What the document shows |
|---|---|
| Two months of till data, competitor check, supplier information | ✓ |
| Prices stay below the competitor midpoint | ✓ |
| +£810/week, £42,000/yr | Ignores the 12% beef rise (up to −£280/wk) and possibly VAT |
| Main-course margin rises to ~71% | Only before the beef rise; ~69–70% after |
| Risotto has "the weakest margin" | **Highest** margin (80%) |
| Risotto has the lowest sales | Tied with specials at 90 |
| Eight-week monitoring gives early warning | Jan–Feb baseline is seasonally weak, so a fall in demand could be missed |

## Recommendations

1. **Drop or rethink the risotto removal.** If the menu needs refreshing, consider promoting the risotto instead, or adding a seasonal special *alongside* it.
2. **Include the beef cost rise** in the projection, using actual beef costs per plate from the kitchen.
3. **State whether margins exclude VAT**, and recalculate if they don't.
4. **Add a break-even volume analysis** for each price rise.
5. **Monitor against the same period last year**, not January–February.
6. **Correct "six trading days" to five.**

The price increases themselves look justified: prices are lowest in the area, they haven't changed since 2024, and beef costs are rising. With the corrections above, the owners can approve them knowing what they'll actually deliver.
